gist: Jihadist groups are shifting from global attacks to local power struggles and tactical compromises.
Groups like JNIM and al-Shabab are adopting rebranding and alliance strategies.
Experts debate whether this pragmatism represents genuine moderation or a strategic Trojan horse.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Jihadist movements are changing shape a quarter of a century after the 9/11 attacks and 12 years after the Islamic State declared its caliphate. Rather than focusing solely on attacking the West or pursuing global jihad, groups like al-Qaeda's Sahel branch JNIM and Somali branch al-Shabab are focusing on local power. They are rebranding, providing aid, forming local alliances, and dropping familiar global jihadist slogans to win over local populations.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: This shift is inspired by the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan and Syria's president Ahmed al-Sharaa, who used pragmatism and local alliances to rise to power. A debate is growing within the jihadist movement between hardliners who reject compromise and pragmatists who see cooperation as a pathway to gaining control.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: It remains unclear whether pragmatic approaches will genuinely moderate these groups or serve as a Trojan horse strategy to secure power. Meanwhile, groups like the Islamic State reject compromise entirely and maintain global ambitions.

sections.text: A court in Düsseldorf granted Fender copyright protection for the Stratocaster design after a Chinese seller did not appear. Fender then launched a campaign sending cease and desist letters to retailers and manufacturers to stop making and selling Strat lookalikes in Europe. In response, German musical instrument retailer Thomann started legal action against Fender, and Fender subsequently sued Thomann for copyright infringement.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The dispute creates intense concern in the guitar world because the Stratocaster shape has been widely copied by countless manufacturers since the 1960s and is considered a generic design by many. sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Legal cases are continuing in Germany as Thomann seeks legal clarity for the wider guitar industry. Meanwhile, Fender stated it remains confident in the original Düsseldorf court judgement and is focusing more on targeting larger manufacturers while listening to smaller builders.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: US stock market indices fell on Wednesday, with the Nasdaq dropping almost 4%. Shares in major technology companies including Nvidia, Anthropic, Amazon, Tesla and SpaceX, Micrsoft and Meta all declined. The US government also announced new tariffs under President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Investors are concerned about the sustainability of massive AI investments. Market volatility has also been driven by Democrat gains in the US midterm elections and turmoil surrounding Nvidia boss Jensen Huang following his temporary resignation.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Democrat politicians have campaigned for tougher AI regulation and a data centre moratorium. Investment bank Goldman Sachs expects AI investment to exceed $1 trillion in 2026.
